newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan says discord with Peru over hostage crisis.
newsitem.headline: Japan says discord with Peru over hostage crisis.

text.p: Japan said on Friday there is a difference of opinion between Tokyo and Lima over the handling of the hostage crisis in Peru that is hampering the search for a solution.

"Japan and Peru are far apart in ideas," top government spokesman Seiroku Kajiyama said, adding there were also some subtle differences between Japan and other countries involved about the best course of action.

He did not elaborate on the problem, but said the difference of approach was holding back progress towards a solution. "There will be no major progress unless those differences are adjusted," Kajiyama told reporters.

Japan, calling Tuesday night's hostage-taking an "unprecedented and extremely serious" incident, has said that protecting the lives of the captives should take the highest priority in resolving the standoff at the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima.
This has been seen by some as a signal that Tokyo wants the Peruvian government to consider striking a deal with the guerrillas, who are demanding the release of jailed comrades.

The heavily armed Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) guerrillas captured the ambassador's home during a party in honour of the Japanese emperor's birthday, seizing hundreds of diplomats, dignitaries, business and government leaders. Some hostages have since been released, leaving around 400 captives still inside the building.
Japanese Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda held talks with Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori in Lima and was also liaising with ambassadors from other countries caught up in the hostage drama.
In a letter to U.S. President Bill Clinton, Fujimori promised on Thursday that the safety of hostages will be his first priority.

"I want to assure your excellency that I am occupying myself permanently and jointly with my team to achieve a solution as soon as possible to this crisis, the principal objective being the safeguarding of the health and life of those who are inside," Fujimori wrote in the letter.

Fujimori, who has ignored an ultimatum by the rebels to mediate in person, has held three emergency cabinet meetings but has not made a public statement to the Peruvian people since the crisis began on Tuesday night.
The rebels have threatened to kill their captives if the Peruvian government does not release up to 500 of their jailed comrades.
At a news conference on Friday, Japan's Vice Foreign Minister Masahiko Komura was quizzed about speculation the United States may push for a hard line with the hostage-takers.
Komura said he believed Washington would oppose giving in to the guerrillas' demands, but that there was no sign the United States was seeking tough action.
The United States on Thursday sent a team of security advisers to Lima to help the U.S. ambassador there deal with the crisis.

"The case is unprecedented and extremely serious...not only Japanese, but numerous people from all over the world are held hostage and our government will make utmost efforts for a peaceful resolution, with the top priority on protecting the lives of the hostages," Komura said.
